newsitem.title: FRANCE: Le Monde interview with BoF's Gerard -Translation.
newsitem.headline: Le Monde interview with BoF's Gerard -Translation.

text.p: Following is a translation of the interview with Jean-Pierre Gerard of the Bank of France's monetary policy council in an advance copy of the edition of Le Monde which will appear later today. It is an unofficial translation by Reuters.

Le Monde: Former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing recently called for a depreciation of the franc versus the mark to help growth in a proposal which revived debate on monetary policy in France. What do you think of his remarks?

Gerard: There have been many analyses in the wake of the remarks from Valery Giscard d'Estaing on the level of European currencies versus the dollar. He is being taken to task for upsetting the markets. These criticiems are unjustified in my view. I think it is natural in a democratic system to worry about the future of our country. That's what he's talking about when he questions the franc-mark parity and above all the parity between the franc and dollar. This is all the more worthwhile in that I believe the Germans are not sufficiently aware of the problems which their monetary policy can have on the launch of the single currency.
LM: What is it that you fault in Germany monetary policy?

Gerard: We will not get away without a frank explanation with Germany. Things have to be said clearly, in a constructive manner without necessarily criticising. In the current state of things and solely in relation to Germany, the pivot rate between the franc and the mark poses no problem, but what is dramatic is the undervaluation versus the dollar.

The Germans say they are happy with a relationship where the dollar stands at 1.53 versus the mark, in other words about 5.13 versus the franc. At the same time, France and Germany's economic structures are not identical. We suffer a lot more from the undervaluation of the dollar and a correct parity for us would be around six francs. If you take 6.25 francs for a dollar and you keep the pivot rate of 3.35 francs for a mark, the mark should then exchange for the dollar at a rate of around 1.87. There's a genuine imbalance and there should be negotiation on the subject.

The Germans must take account of the economic differences between countries and acknowledge that our interests must be defended and that our country faces a difficult social and political situation with the undervaluation of the dollar.

With two years to go to the single currency deadline, it is surprising that there have not been talks on the overvaluation of European currencies versus the dollar. Without this, we will have serious problems bringing this monetary union process to fruition and above all big problems managing the single currency afterwards.
LM: What ways do you see of counterbalancing the dollar undervaluation?

Gerard: There are three solutions. The first would consist of using all our margin of manoeuvre and lowering short-term rates in France and Germany. The issue is making the dollar more attractive versus the mark. It might not be enough, but it would already be a step in the right direction. Unfortunately we have little influence on German monetary policy.

A second possibility, given that we cannot get a concerted reduction in rates, would be to modify the franc-mark parity. That is the reasoning of Giscard d'Estaing. It is probably a less good solution since we are already overcompetitive compared to Germany, but German lack of understanding may make it necessary.

The third solution would be to make monetary and trade policy more coherent. Let's have a community (EU) preference to counter an aggressive U.S. trade policy founded on depreciation of the dollar. Perhaps a mix of the three solutions will be needed.
LM: Do you not have the feeling of breaking a taboo by directly attacking German monetary policy and 'selfishness'?

Gerard: I have a lot of respect for the Germans. On monetary issues, it is not a question of starting a battle, but of having a policy adapted to the economic situation. In France, we have the failing of believing that everything that happens in Germany is fine. Even if Germany still has its economic merits, its industrial fabric is eroding, it has a considerable level of unemployment, its labour costs are well above ours, work hours are shorter and its external trade balance is less favourable than in the past. They are clinging to their monetary policy of mark stability but I do not believe this is the reason for their past success. It is rather the result of it.
LM: does that mean you believe that it's indispensible to have a weak euro?

Gerard: I have always been surprised to hear the Germans saying they favour a strong euro. I do not know what a strong euro is. Is the dollar strong or weak? In any case it carries relatively low interest rates. A stable euro will be a currency which will not lose its value, goes hand-in-hand with weak inflation and in which people have confidence. That will be sufficient.
LM: Are you bothered by the Bundesbank's criticisms, notably on the French budget and the awkward silence of the French?

Gerard: On budget policy, I am not sure that the Germans are in a position to give us a lesson. They got into some dubious budget practices with the takeover of the Treuhand, the German agency for the privatisation of east German companies. And it is not certain either that they will fulfil the Maastricht criteria in 1997.
LM: Do you favour Italy's entry into the euro and do you see in such an event a way of having a weaker euro versus the dollar?

Gerard: If Italy meets the Maastricht criteria, there is no reason for it not to participate in the single currency. That's the answer on the technical side. There is a more political response. It would be extremely damaging to take such a crucial step in Europe without Italy, who has been with us since the Treaty of Rome. There's a problem of loyalty to history. They wanted the construction of Europe, with the Germans and the French. It would be a mistake to create a euro without them.

The question is not whether these are countries we are happy with but whether they will meet the criteria. At the time of Italy's re-entry into the ERM, Germany gave too much the impression that it did not want Italy. From the point where a certain degree of flexibility will be used for certain countries, as the treaty allows, it has to be applied to other countries.
LM: The renewal mandate for the make-up of the Bank of France's monetary policy council is fuelling speculation about possible change in monetary policy. Do you favour that?

Gerard: Monetary policy cannot be looked on in terms of a switch. We have a mandate which is clear- the fight against inflation. But there can be nuances in line with the way in which the various risks are assessed by the members of the monetary policy council. It is plausible for example to think that the risks of inflation are slight in the coming years.

Moreover, social risks have to be take account of. Some are more sensitive to this within the council than others. Altering the council could introduce certain nuances. If unemployment keeps rising, something will happen in the end. We are already witnessing extreme structural transformation such as areas outside legal control, parallel economic acitivity. We are in a profoundly unstable situation. The Bank of France's mission against inflation will lose its meaning if social troubles break out.
LM: Does franc depreciation carry inflation risks?

Gerard: Probably not. However, a depreciation of the franc vis-a-vis the mark is not desirable since this would increase market interest rates. Nevertheless, there is an optimum balance that has to found between interest rates and exchange rates. In my view, this has not been reached today. In other words, are we not paying very dearly for having the lowest long term interest rates in the world when you take the dollar's weakness into account? It is not by systematically seeking the lowest interest rates in the world that you find this optimum balance.
LM: What kind of turn in monetary policy can we expect?

Gerard: We could use the full margin of manoeuvre available to us within the framework of a balance with Germany. We could also take account of a situation which has changed profoundly in France, which has shown a significant trade surplus for several years. It is perhaps possible, therefore, to consider going a bit further in the reduction of rates. We are perhaps underestimating ourt own strengths and overestimating those of Germany. In any case, if we want to build Europe, we have to build it together, on the political, economic, social and cultural level.
-- Paris Newsroom +33 1 4221 5452
